analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to any resident who can't get affordable coverage elsewhere, with subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote, dying when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let each state allow residents who aren't already on Medicaid or other coverage to buy into the state's Medicaid plan, paying premiums capped at 9.5% of income and using the same Affordable Care Act tax credits available for private plans. It would also pay primary care providers who treat Medicaid patients at Medicare rates, send states $100 billion in grants to expand access to care, and give full federal matching funds to any state that expands Medicaid no matter when it does so. Each state would decide whether to offer the buy-in; the federal government would not force any state to participate.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults who earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford private plans would get a cheaper, publicly run option, as long as their state chooses to offer it. People in areas with no ACA marketplace silver plans could use buy-in coverage as the benchmark for tax credits. Medicaid patients would benefit from higher payments to primary care providers, which typically improves access to doctors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured adults in states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Lets residents not eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage buy into their state's Medicaid plan starting January 1, 2018, with premiums capped at 9.5% of family income [S2][S3].
Makes buy-in coverage eligible for ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, with the state Medicaid agency treated like a marketplace plan issuer [S2][S3].
Requires Medicaid primary care payments at no less than Medicare Part B rates for physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified nurse-midwives [S2][S3].
Appropriates $100 billion for state grants to improve Medicaid provider access and $200 million for access metrics, with at least 10% of grant funds usable to set up the buy-in program [S3].
Gives the enhanced federal Medicaid match to any state that expands coverage to newly eligible adults, regardless of when it expands, removing the penalty for late expander states [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost of the $100 billion in grants, the 90% federal match for buy-in administration, higher Medicaid primary care payments, and enhanced matching funds for late-expanding states. Private insurers selling ACA marketplace plans would lose potential customers in states that offer the cheaper public option.

drawbacks.text: Coverage would be voluntary for states, so whether you could buy in would depend entirely on where you live; states could also restrict enrollment to marketplace open-enrollment periods [S3].

The bill appropriates large new federal funds — $100 billion in state grants, a 90% federal match for buy-in administration, and Medicare-rate payments for Medicaid primary care — adding substantially to federal health spending [S3].

Medicaid networks often pay doctors less and include fewer providers than private plans, so buy-in enrollees could face access limits unless the provider payment provisions succeed in widening networks [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a lower-cost public coverage option for people who fall through the cracks, with the same subsidies available for private plans. The tradeoffs are the federal cost and the state-by-state design, which would leave millions in non-participating states without the option and could produce uneven access depending on where they live. The provider payment floor is a good-faith attempt to fix Medicaid's known weakness of narrow networks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Ray Luján introduced the State Public Option Act on October 25, 2017, joined by two dozen original Democratic cosponsors [S3][S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and three days later to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no vote ever occurred; the congressional record shows no action after the subcommittee referral [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers selling marketplace plans were better off, because no cheaper public competitor was created, and the Republican House majority avoided a vote on a public coverage option.

industries.industry: Private health insurers selling ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: Buy-in Medicaid coverage would be a cheaper public alternative to marketplace plans, and buy-in enrollees' plans would be treated as the benchmark silver plan for setting subsidies, pressuring private plan prices [S3]. Insurers would lose potential customers in states that adopt the buy-in.

industries.industry: Primary care providers (physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, nurse-midwives)
industries.note: The bill requires Medicaid primary care payments at no less than Medicare Part B rates and lets states use grants to raise provider payment rates, addressing the common complaint that Medicaid pays doctors too little to see patients [S3].

Buy-in enrollees can be covered through Medicaid managed care contracts, so plans would gain members in opt-in states, but those contracts would have to pay primary care providers at the Medicare-rate floor and document compliance [S3].

States get a 90% federal match for buy-in administration, up to $100 billion in access grants usable partly for buy-in setup, and restored enhanced matching funds for late Medicaid expansion [S2][S3].
